analysis.one_liner: Bans forced-arbitration clauses that block investors from suing brokers in court.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Brokerage firms and investment advisers commonly write clauses into customer contracts requiring any dispute to go to private arbitration and barring class action lawsuits. This bill would make those clauses illegal, letting investors choose between arbitration and court — including class actions — when they are defrauded. It also would stop companies from putting mandatory arbitration into shareholder agreements.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors. Under current contracts, someone whose broker cheats them is generally locked into a private arbitration process chosen by the firm and cannot join a class action. This bill would restore the choice to go to court, either alone or with other investors, and would void those clauses in existing agreements too.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits brokers, dealers, and investment advisers from including mandatory arbitration, forum restrictions, or class action bans in customer agreements, and voids such provisions in existing agreements [S2][S3].
Bars companies from mandating arbitration in shareholder agreements and prohibits registering securities from issuers that do so [S2][S3].
The bill's findings state that mandatory arbitration clauses leverage firms' advantages to severely restrict defrauded investors from seeking redress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and securities issuers, who would face lawsuits in court — including class actions — that arbitration clauses currently shield them from, and who would bear higher litigation exposure and costs.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is often faster and cheaper than court for individual investors, and FINRA arbitration would remain available as a voluntary choice; the bill's critics could argue courts add cost and delay for small claims [S3].
Class actions frequently deliver large fees to plaintiffs' lawyers while individual class members recover little, so opening the courtroom door does not guarantee investors get meaningful recoveries.
Firms facing more court exposure could pass higher compliance and litigation costs on to customers through fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For investors with real losses, the gain is substantial: access to court, public records, and class actions that make small individual claims worth pursuing. The costs — slower resolution in some cases and more litigation expense for firms — are real but fall mostly on the industry side of the ledger. The bill preserves voluntary arbitration, which answers the fairness objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on April 15, 2021 with five Democratic cosponsors joining as original sponsors [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction; no further action was ever taken [S5].
All six cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brokerage firms, investment advisers, and securities issuers keep mandatory arbitration clauses, so defrauded investors remain largely confined to firm-selected arbitration with no class actions. Committee inaction on a bill with no Republican support meant the industry's existing legal shield stayed intact for the Congress.
